# Renal hemodynamic evaluation protocol based on the pathophysiological mechanism of acute kidney injury: Critical Care UltraSound Guided-A(KI)BCDE

**Authors:** Lixia Liu; Dawei Liu; Zhenjie Hu; Xiaoting Wang; Yangong Chao; Jun Wu; Wanhong Yin; Hongmin Zhang; Lina Zhang; Wei He; Ran Zhu; Qianghong Xu; Rongli Yang; Yan Huo; Qian Zhang; Haitao Liu; Weihua Zhu; Qian Zhang; Rong Li

**Affiliations:** aDepartment of Critical Care Medicine, The Fourth Hospital of Hebei Medical University, Shijiazhuang, China | bDepartment of Intensive Care Department, Peking Union Medical College Hospital, Beijing, China | cDepartment of Critical Care Medicine, The First Affiliated Hospital of Tsinghua University, Beijing, China | dDepartment of Ruijin Hospital, Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, Shanghai, China | eDepartment of Intensive Care, West China Hospital, Sichuan University, Chengdu, China | fDepartment of Critical Care Medicine, Xiangya Hospital, Central South University, Changsha, China | gDepartment of Intensive Care Medicine, Beijing Tongren Hospital, Capital Medical University, Beijing, China | hDepartment of Intensive Care Medicine, The First Affiliated Hospital of China Medical University, Shenyang, China | iDepartment of Critical Care Medicine, Zhejiang Hospital, Hangzhou, China | jDepartment of Critical Care Medicine, The Central Hospital of Dalian, Dalian, China | kDepartment of Intensive Care Medicine, Affiliated Hospital of Guizhou Medical University, Guiyang, China | lDepartment of Critical Care Medicine, The Fourth Hospital of Harbin Medical University, Harbin, China | mDepartment of Intensive Care Medicine, The First Affiliated Hospital of Kunming Medical University, Kunming, China

## Abstract

The multiple etiological characteristics of acute kidney injury (AKI) have brought great challenges to its clinical diagnosis and treatment. Renal injury in critically ill patients always indicates hemodynamic injury. The Critical Care UltraSound Guided (CCUSG)-A(KI)BCDE protocol developed by the Chinese Critical Ultrasound Study Group (CCUSG), respectively, includes A(KI) diagnosis and risk assessment and uses B-mode ultrasound, Color doppler ultrasound, spectral Doppler ultrasound, and contrast Enhanced ultrasound to obtain the hemodynamic characteristics of the kidney so that the pathophysiological mechanism of the occurrence and progression of AKI can be captured and the prognosis of AKI can be predicted combined with other clinical information; therefore, the corresponding intervention and treatment strategies can be formulated to achieve targeted, protocolized, and individualized therapy.

## Background

Acute kidney injury (AKI) occurs in more than half of critically ill patients and is an independent risk factor for poor prognosis. AKI is a complex clinical syndrome encompassing a wide spectrum of etiologies, such as sepsis, volume depletion, inflammation, ischemia-reperfusion injury, exogenous and endogenous toxins, surgery, obstruction, heart failure, and others. These various triggers often coexist in one patient simultaneously, therefore making it very challenging to identify the etiologies and relevant therapeutic targets. The current diagnostic criteria, biomarkers [1–3], and electronic alarming systems [4,5] are not appropriately used in identifying the etiology of AKI and guiding the treatment.

A series of studies have confirmed that renal hemodynamic alterations in critically ill patients is an independent risk factor for the occurrence and progression of AKI [6–10]. Thanks to the advantage of perfect morphological integration, the function of point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS), and the availability of smaller and cost-effective ultrasound machines, the combination of evidence collected can better equip the non-radiologists and non-cardiologists, making them more competent in performing POCUS; therefore, this method is currently applied in many clinical settings and in all phases of care—from screening and diagnosis to procedural guidance and monitoring; its application has been associated with the changes in clinical decision making in medical practice [11,12]. Professional societies such as the International Liaison Committee on Lung Ultrasound [13], the American Society of Echocardiography [14], and the Chinese Critical Ultrasound Study Group (CCUSG) [15,16] have established guidelines on the use of POCUS; thus, POCUS will be used as a standard diagnostic tool for all clinicians [17]. The CCUSG developed a Critical-Care UltraSound Guided (CCUSG)-A(KI)BCDE protocol (Figure 1); using proven ultrasonic techniques, including two-dimensional (2D) ultrasound, doppler ultrasound and contrast-enhanced ultrasound, the renal anatomical structure and renal blood perfusion were evaluated to obtain comprehensive renal hemodynamic information, as well as the pathophysiological mechanisms of the occurrence and progression of AKI. Under critical ultrasound guidance [15], targeted and protocolized management can be implemented. This article aimed to describe in detail the method of implementing the CCUSG-A(KI)BCDE protocol, which can provide support and guidance for clinicians, reduce the occurrence of AKI, and improve the prognosis of patients with AKI.

*Figure 1.: Critical Care UltraSound-Guided (CCUSG)-A(KI)BCDE protocol. AKI: acute kidney injury; MAP: mean arterial pressure; CO: cardiac output; IAP: intra-abdominal pressure; CVP: Central venous pressure.*

## AKI diagnosis and risk assessment of AKI occurrence and progression

Identifying AKI and determining the risk factors for its occurrence and progression is the initial step.

### Diagnosis of AKI

AKI is diagnosed according to the Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) guidelines [1].

### Present and past history of illness

Present illness such as sepsis, shock, major bleeding, and acute cardiac failure and recent surgeries (e.g., cardiothoracic surgery and upper abdominal surgery), as well as past illnesses like hypertension and diabetes and long-term use of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, chronic cardiac failure, chronic kidney disease (CKD), and renal replacement therapy (RRT) can all lead to the occurrence and progression of AKI by impairment of renal hemodynamics through various mechanisms [18].

## B-mode ultrasound

Organ structure determines organ function.

### Examination method

A convex probe with a frequency of 2.5–5 MHz is typically used. The examination is performed based on two basic planes (coronal plane and transverse plane) (Figure 2A,B). It includes size (length, width, thickness), internal measurements (parenchyma thickness, cortex thickness, and tubular inner diameter in the collective system), echogenicity (cortex, medulla, and collective system), and others (stone, tumor, cyst, abscess, and so on).

*Figure 2.: Two-dimensional ultrasonography of the kidneys. (A) Ultrasound image of a normal kidney, coronal plane. (B) Ultrasound image of a normal kidney, transverse plane. (C) Ultrasonography of acute kidney injury (AKI): a 59-year-old man, on the third day after Colon cancer surgery, had an abdominal infection and sepsis-associated AKI. The two-dimensional ultrasonography showed a slight increase in renal volume, parenchymal thickening, and increased cortical echogenicity. (D) Ultrasonography of chronic kidney disease (CKD): an 85-year-old woman with chronic renal insufficiency, severe pneumonia, heart failure, and AKI—a complication of CKD; the two-dimensional ultrasound indicated a significant reduction in the kidney volume, thinning of the parenchyma, blurry structure of the cortex and medulla, and increased cortical echogenicity. E. Ultrasonography of hydronephrosis: a 47-year-old woman with extensive metastases in the peritoneal cavity from ovarian cancer, right ureter compression, ureteral obstruction, renal pelvis dilation, and renal cortex thinning. F. Ultrasound image of the kidney cyst: a 69-year-old woman with AKI after rectal tumor surgery; polycystic kidney disease was diagnosed 12 years ago, and two-dimensional ultrasound showed multiple hypoechoic thin-walled cysts in the kidney.*

### Normal 2D ultrasonography

The normal ultrasound image is shown in Figure 2A. The kidneys are oval. Adult kidneys have a long axis diameter of 9–12 cm, a width of 5–7 cm, and a thickness of 4–5 cm. The parenchyma and cortex thickness are about 1–2 cm and 0.8–1 cm respectively. The cortex is equal-echo or slightly less than hepatic echo, while the medulla is hypoecho. The border between the cortex and medulla is relatively clear. Renal sinus accounts for about 1/2–2/3 of the kidney with hyper and heterogeneous echo. A tubular liquid dark area with a diameter of <1 cm may be seen within the sinus (Figure 2A).

### Pathophysiological and clinical significance of renal morphology

In some degree, the kidney volume, especially the thickness of the renal parenchyma reflects the numbers of functional nephrons. The fewer normal nephrons, the more impairment of renal function regardless of the subtypes of AKI. Volume enlargement and parenchymal thickening with increased echogenicity are often suggestive of acute lesions (Figure 2C). On the contrary, reduced volume and thinned parenchyma with increased echogenicity are often suggestive of chronic lesions (Figure 2D).

Three-dimensional ultrasound method such as Crislip GR [19] was used to evaluate the renal volume of rats with various durations of ischemia-reperfusion injury; results showed that ischemic durations of 15, 30, and 45 min resulted in a graded increase in kidney volume (Ptime 0.001) with a positively linear correlation between renal volume and the degree of renal tubular injury, which was superior to serum creatinine in terms of detection capability. In a small study of 26 patients with acute tubular necrosis, Nomura and others [20] demonstrated that the kidney size, especially the anteroposterior diameter, were positively correlated with serum creatinine and length of hospitalization. Cortical thickness and glomerular filtration rate (GFR) are well correlated with the stage of CKD and can be used to evaluate the phase and progression of CKD [21,22].

It should be pointed out that an abnormal kidney morphology mostly indicates renal histological and function disorders; however, a normal morphology under 2D ultrasonography does not necessarily indicate a healthy kidney; many patients with AKI present normal kidney volume, thickness, and echogenicity under conventional 2D ultrasonography.

## Color doppler ultrasound

Organ blood flow perfusion guarantees organ function, which is especially true of the kidneys [23].

Renal Blood Flow (RBF) accounts for 20%–25% of CO. RBF is not aimed at achieving self-survival but cleansing the metabolic wastes; regulating water, electrolyte, and acid-base; maintaining homeostasis; and regulating blood pressure and other important functions. Decreased renal blood perfusion suggests a reduction in the volume of blood that is filtrated, metabolized, and regulated by the kidneys; it is manifested as a disorder in the water, electrolyte, and acid-base balance, etc. When a certain level is reached, it is clinically defined as AKI. Color doppler flow mapping can intuitively display the conditions of renal blood perfusion, including the amount and the area of perfusion.

However, we need to note that although renal blood perfusion is a guarantee of kidney function, it is not the only factor determining kidney function, such as septic AKI is a typical representative [6,24]. Because the pathogenesis of septic AKI determines that renal blood perfusion is different in different periods, which may be normal or even increased in the early stage, and may be reduced in the late stage, with or without the redistribution from the medulla to cortex, which is also related to the severity of septic AKI In fact, all other types of AKI have similar characteristics, that is, the primary disease will lead to a certain degree of damage to the kidney itself, that is, blood perfusion is the fundamental guarantee, but it is not the only factor [6] In addition, due to the individual differences of each patient, even in the face of the same pathogenic factor, each patient’s response will be different, AKI performance will be different, and blood ­perfusion will be different. This is why we recommend a comprehensive evaluation, including both macro- and microcirculation [25].

### Examination method

Based on 2D ultrasound, color doppler mode is used.

### Normal color doppler ultrasound image

On normal color doppler ultrasound, the renal blood is observed flowing directly from the renal hilum to the renal cortex, filled the kidney (Figure 3D).

*Figure 3.: Semi-quantitative grading of renal blood flow distribution. (A) Grade 0, there is no blood flow to the kidneys. (B) Grade 1, a small volume of blood is flowing to the renal hilum. (C) Grade 2, most parts of the renal parenchyma are filled with blood. (D) Grade 3, the renal parenchyma is filled with blood. White arrow, interlobar artery. White arrowhead, interlobar vein.*

### Semi-quantitative grading of RBF distribution and its clinical application

The renal blood flow is classified into four grades: Grade 0, no blood flow in the kidney (Figure 3A); Grade 1, a small volume of blood flow in the renal hilum (Figure 3B); Grade 2, blood flowing to most parts of the renal parenchyma (Figure 3C); and Grade 3, normal renal blood flow to the cortex, filled (Figure 3D). This classification not only directly shows the renal blood perfusion, but can also be used to predict the occurrence of AKI within 24 h [26,27].

## Spectral doppler ultrasound

To a certain extent, the renal arteriovenous doppler waveforms and the corresponding renal resistive index (RRI) and venous impedance index (VII) can reflect the pathophysiological mechanisms and etiology of renal disease, guide treatment, and predict the prognosis.

### Renal artery assessment

#### Examination method

Steps: The probe with a frequency of 2.5–5 MHz is selected. The kidney’s maximum coronal section is obtained in 2D mode. Color Doppler is used to identify the renal intrarenal artery. The interlobar artery which walks through the renal column is located (Figure 3D). Pulse Doppler is selected, and the sampling line is placed on the blood flow, parallel to the blood flow as much as possible. Approximately 2–5 mm of the sample is acquired, and 3 to 5 similar consecutive waveforms are obtained in one breathing cycle. The peak systolic velocity rate and end diastolic velocity rate are measured in every 3 waveforms. The RRI is calculated as follows: RRI = (peak systolic velocity minus end diastolic velocity divided by peak systolic velocity. Then, the mean value is selected. The contralateral kidney is examined to obtain the RRI.

#### Renal artery waveform type and RRI

There are three types of renal artery waveform. The normal has a typical low resistance pattern, which is characterized by a rapid increase in systolic blood flow velocity and a slow decline in the diastolic phase. The diastolic flow velocity is 30%–50% of the systolic flow velocity with an RRI value of 0.5–0.7 (Figure 4A). The small slow wave (Figure 4B) indicates that the blood flow velocity is slow during systole and diastole, and a high resistance wave can be manifested as a rapid increase in the blood flow velocity during systole, and a quick drop or even disappearance of blood flow during diastole (Figure 4C,D). Both small slow wave and high-resistance wave are abnormal spectra, with RRI value of <0.5 and >0.7, respectively.

*Figure 4.: Waveform of renal arterial blood flow. (A) Normal renal interlobar artery waveform and renal resistance index value. (B) Small slow wave: a 37-year-old woman, a significant decrease in renal artery blood supply caused by aortic dissection; the blood flow in the proximal left renal artery from the abdominal aorta was almost interrupted; the distal wave of the interrupted blood flow showed a slow rise during systole, decreased peak value, and gradual decrease during diastole. (C–E) High-resistance wave: images shown in (B,C) are captured from the same patient. (C) shows the significantly reduced renal blood flow and a high-resistance waveform from the renal segmental artery; (D) shows a 31-year-old man with acute severe pancreatitis complicated with intra-abdominal hypertension and acute kidney injury, an intra-abdominal pressure (IAP) of 25 mmHg, and a nail-shaped waveform from the renal segmental artery, with diastolic blood flow interruption. The image shown in (E) is captured from the same patient. (E) shows the renal artery blood flow spectrum when IAP reduced to 12 mmHg after continuous renal replacement therapy. Compared with (D), (E) shows an increase in the peak systolic flow velocity, visible diastolic blood flow but significantly reduced blood flow velocity during diastole compared with that during systole, and a high-resistance waveform.*

#### Generation principle and influencing factors of renal artery waveform and RRI

Arterial Doppler waveform analysis is based on the changes in blood flow velocity caused by pulsatile arterial perfusion. The ratio of diastolic to systolic blood velocity is mainly determined based on the downstream resistance [28]. As resistance increases, the diastolic velocity decreases compared with the systolic velocity. However, the correlation between RRI and vascular resistance was influenced by multiple factors; thus, the use of RRI to guide blood pressure titration in shock patients was limited, among which vascular compliance, pulse pressure (PP), renal interstitial pressure, and distal vascular bed area are the main influential factors [29,30].

Vascular compliance directly determines the influence of resistance on RRI. The higher the compliance, the more the RRI was affected by resistance. In the absence of compliance, the RRI was independent of vascular resistance [31]. Age is a common factor affecting compliance, both younger and older age can lead to decreased vascular compliance. The RRI was ≥0.70 in patients aged ≤4 years. The RRI increases with age, especially in individuals aged 40 years and older [29,32,33]. Hypertension and diabetes often lead to decreased renal artery compliance, which may not affect the baseline RRI values, but reduce the RRI response to MAP changes in these patients [34]. Further increases in MAP may not confer additional benefit due to the reduced RRI response to MAP [35]. Renal interstitial pressure essentially reflects renal vascular compliance (the pressure difference between the intrarenal vessels and extrarenal vessels); renal interstitial pressure is positively correlated with RRI.

RRI increases as the cross-sectional area of the distal arterial bed decreases, and this effect is independent of the vascular compliance and RRI.

#### Clinical application of renal artery waveform and RRI

A comprehensive understanding of the generation principle and influencing factors of renal artery waveform and RRI is the basic premise for their appropriate clinical application, which needs to be integrated with the hemodynamic assessment of renal veins, renal microcirculation, and the body’s systemic circulations; empirical application often leads to unsatisfactory clinical outcomes.

#### Identify the etiologies

#### Small slow waveform: an RRI of <0.5

The main mechanism for its formation is the significant reduction in blood flow. It occurs more often in downstream of the remarkably narrow segment of the extrarenal artery and less often in the intrarenal arteries, especially the arterioles (Figure 4B). Obstruction removal is the key therapeutic strategy.

#### High-resistance waveform: an RRI of >0.7

The main mechanism for its formation is high blood flow resistance. Unlike small slow waveform, it occurs more frequently in the intrarenal arteries and the upstream of the remarkably narrow segment of the extrarenal artery. The common pathophysiological mechanisms in critically ill patients are renal vasoconstriction caused by renal hypoperfusion, decreased vascular compliance caused by increased renal interstitial pressure, and decreased distal vascular bed area caused by microcirculation disorders. The common etiologies are sepsis, cardiac dysfunction, hypovolemia, hypervolemia, inflammatory response, high intra-abdominal pressure, etc.

#### Titrate blood pressure

Titrate the optimal MAP by adjusting the dose of the vasopressors, and then select the MAP with the lowest RRI.

Although a number of factors influence the correlation between RRI and vascular resistance, MAP still has a positive correlation with RRI [36–38]. Remember that other causes of increased RRI should be addressed prior to MAP titration as far as possible since high dosages of norepinephrine can potentially cause cardiomyocyte damage, oxidative stress, and sepsis-related immunosuppression [39]. Certainly, vasopressors can be adjusted at the same time when the problem cannot be resolved immediately.

An elevated MAP may also lead to overperfusion in other organs, such as the cerebrum, especially when the autonomic regulation of cerebral blood flow is impaired [40]. At this time, the cerebral perfusion must be evaluated.

#### Guide fluid resuscitation

If the RRI is reduced after fluid resuscitation, it makes sense to resuscitate, otherwise it may increase the risk of fluid overload.

The goal of fluid resuscitation is to improve tissue perfusion by increasing CO and MAP, while the dissociation between the systemic and the renal response to fluid challenge was notable. Moussa et al. showed that fluid administration can result in a small but consistent decrease in RI, which were better predictors of an increase in urine output than were MAP and PP [41]. Ferré et al. also showed similar results. They found that a fluid challenge can decrease RRI in suspected hypovolaemia patients at risk of postoperative AKI, but the changes are not correlated to changes in CO [42]. While Schnell et al. did not find the same results, which would be due to the definition of the fluid responsiveness they used. They used an increase in descending aortic blood flow, a systemic response, to define the response of fluid challenge [43].

#### RRT management

In AKI, when RRI is <0.7, RRT not likely required; if RRI remains at ≥0.7 even after conventional treatment [44], which means that the renal pathophysiological status and function might not improve [44] and RRT is likely to be initiated. During RRT, a decreased RRI indicates a better prognosis. When the RRI is <0.7, successful discontinuation of RRT is highly likely. If the RRI remains ≥0.7 despite the recovery of renal function and successful discontinuation of RRT, which indicates that the renal pathological state has not been completely corrected. Hemodynamic instability is a common phenomenon during RRT and is associated with poor prognosis [45,46]. Hypotension occurring within 1 h after initiation of Continuous RRT (CRRT) is an independent risk factor for poor prognosis [46]. The RRI helps guide MAP setting [36–38], fluid resuscitation and volume management [41,42].

#### Predict the prognosis

Many studies have confirmed the predictive utility of RRI in AKI. Lerolle et al. [37]used RRI for the first time to predict the prognosis of critically ill patients and discovered that whether the occurrence or progression of AKI presents on the 5th day after septic shock was associated with a first day RRI of >0.74, and is not related with the presence or severity of AKI on day 1 [37]. A series of subsequent studies found that patients with an RRI of >0.70 had 29.85 times increased risk of persistent AKI [47], which was an independent risk factor for renal function deterioration after 1 year in patients with chronic cardiac insufficiency [48]; an RRI of >0.77 in patients with AKI was associated with an increased risk of death [49]. An RRI of ≥0.80 at least 3 months after kidney transplantation was closely related to graft dysfunction and mortality [50].

### Renal vein assessment

#### Method of obtaining the renal venous waveform

The method of obtaining the renal venous waveform is like that of renal artery assessment, but slightly different because the renal vein is highly compliant and susceptible to respiration. Therefore, the selection of 3 end-expiratory spectrum samples in the same respiratory cycle is recommended especially when taking deep breaths.

#### Renal venous waveform pattern and VII

Renal venous waveform has two types: continuous (patterns A, B, and C) and discontinuous (patterns D, E, and F). VII is a measure of vein pulsatility and is calculated based on the Doppler waveform: maximum velocity minus minimum velocity divided by maximum velocity. A normal waveform is continuous (pattern A) with a certain pulsatility change with a VII of 0.12–0.52 (Figure 5A). Pattern B (Figure 5B) and pattern C (Figure 5C) demonstrate a continuous waveform with either too small or too large pulsatility; these patterns are often found in abnormal waveforms and prone to progress to a discontinuous spectrum, although both can be observed in individuals with a normal kidney function. The discontinuous patterns are abnormal. Interruption or reversal of the end-diastolic blood flow indicates a pattern D (Figure 5D). Interruption or reversal both end-systolic blood flow and end-diastolic blood flow indicates a biphasic pattern E (Figure 5E); meanwhile, a blood flow that only appears during systole or diastole indicates a monophasic pattern (pattern F) (Figure 5F).

*Figure 5.: Renal venous blood flow pattern. (A–C) Continuous pattern. (A) Pattern A, continuous Doppler waveform in the renal interlobar vein. (B) Pattern B, continuous-linear like Doppler waveform in the renal interlobar vein from a 41-year-old female patient with a 4-year history of diabetes because of diabetic ketoacidosis, with a venous impedance index (VII) of <0.12. (C) Pattern C, continuous flow with increased pulsatility in the renal interlobar vein with a VII >0.52. (D–F) Discontinues pattern. (D) Pattern D, end-diastolic flow interruption and/or reversal (white arrow) in the renal interlobar vein. (E) Pattern E (biphasic pattern): both end-systolic blood flow and end-diastolic blood flow were interrupted (white arrows) and/or reversed (green arrows) in the segmental vein from the same patient Figure 5D, the pulsatility of the segmental vein is higher than that of the interlobar vein. (F) Pattern F (monophasic pattern): the blood flow was only observed during the diastolic phase (white arrows).*

#### Renal vein waveform and VII generation principle and influencing factors

Unlike the arterial side, the vascular resistance on the venous side is normally negligible because the veins act as capacitance vessels; therefore, their impedance to blood flow is directly related to compliance. When the renal tissue compliance drops, the amplitude changes occurring throughout the cardiac cycle are suppressed, for example urinary tract obstructive nephropathy [51] (Figure 6A) and diabetic nephropathy [52] (Figure 5B).

*Figure 6.: Amplitude changes in renal venous blood flow waveform in the different renal interstitial pressure. A 46-year-old female patient with stable circulation and normal renal function 1 day after bilateral ovary and tumor resection. The right kidney (A) shows hydronephrosis, while the left kidney (B) is morphologically normal. The waveforms of the interlobar veins in both kidneys showed both continuous and intermittent end-diastolic interruption patterns, and the blood flow velocity and amplitude of the right interlobar veins were lower than those of the left kidney because of the relative higher right renal interstitial pressure. The higher amplitude of the interlobar vein of the left kidney is induced by the relative increased blood perfusion and unchanged interstitial pressure.*

Also because of the high compliance, the blood flow waveform of renal veins is significantly affected by the right atrium pressure (RAP) during a cardiac cycle [52]. Therefore, the normal renal vein waveform is not only continuous, but also changes with the variation of RAP during the cardiac cycle with a VII value between 0.12 and 0.52 (Figure 5A). The increase of RAP leads to the obstruction of renal venous return, and the waveform is interrupted or even reversed, which is most likely to occur in the atrial systole period (Figure 5D). If the pressure is further increased, the back flow is obstructed during the atrial systole and atrial filling periods, and it is manifested as a biphasic waveform (Figure 5E), or even only during the systole or diastolic period, and it is manifested as a uniphasic waveform (Figure 5F), mostly during the diastolic period.

The renal venous flow pattern ultimately depends on the combined effect of RAP and renal tissue compliance.

#### Clinical application of renal vein waveform and VII

Similarly, a comprehensive understanding of the principles and influencing factors of renal vein waveform and VII is the basic prerequisite for their appropriate clinical application, and the empirical application of these factors often leads to unsatisfactory clinical results.

#### Identify the etiologies

Due to the high compliance characteristics of the renal vein, it is highly sensitive to its influencing factors, and the renal vein waveform changes even earlier than that of CVP and the inferior vena cava [53]. Any factors that result in RAP elevation such as fluid overload, tricuspid regurgitation, pulmonary hypertension, or right ventricular (RV) dysfunction, would lead to the obstruction of the renal venous return.

Similarly, any factors that lead to decreased renal compliance such as CKD, diabetes [52] (Figure 5B), urinary tract obstruction [51, 54] (Figure 6A), renal tissue inflammation, and even the interlobar vein due to the relative lower compliance of the renal parenchyma in the normal kidney compared to the renal segmental vein due to relative higher compliance of the collecting system (Figure 5D) would lead to a decrease in the renal venous pulsatility; any factors that can lead to an increase in renal tissue compliance, such as decreased renal perfusion (Figure 6B) and the renal segmental vein in the normal kidney compared to the interlobar vein (Figure 5E).

#### RRT management

Discontinuous renal venous spectrum and increased VII indicates renal venous congestion, which suggests the renal response to diuretics is likely to be reduced; hence, these patients may benefit from RRT along with other indications for RRT and a higher dehydration rate. In patients with normal VII value and continuous renal venous spectrum, dehydration should be cautiously performed to prevent systemic instability; this event can also be an indication to stop RRT during an RRT aiming to dehydration.

#### Predict prognosis

The current studies mainly focuse on the prognosis of patients with heart failure [55–57] or recovering from cardiac surgery [58,59]. The discontinuous renal venous waveform is an ultrasonic index for venous congestion in patients with cardiac dysfunction [55–59], and an independent risk factor for poor prognosis such as readmission, heart transplantation, AKI [58,59] and mortality in patients with heart failure [55–57] or post cardiac surgery [58,59]; it is independent from RAP and serum atrial natriuretic peptide levels [55]. In addition, the risk for poor prognosis increases as the degree of venous congestion increases [8,57–59].

## Contrast-enhanced ultrasound and evaluation

Contrast Enhanced UltraSound (CEUS) is selectively applied according to the needs of illness and the capacity of the department.

After the above ultrasound examination, a final evaluation should be finished.

### CEUS

Renal perfusion alterations, especially at the microvascular level, appear to play a crucial role in AKI occurrence [10]. However, despite optimization of macrovascular hemodynamic parameters, occult renal hypoperfusion may persist with an early AKI [60]. On the other hand, after initial hemodynamic resuscitation, renal function impairment may also occur despite a preserved global RBF [61–66]. Hence, the assessment of the microcirculation alterations is necessary. The waveform of interlobar arteries and veins and the corresponding RRI and VII are usually used to evaluate the resistance of forward perfusion and back flow of renal microcirculation, indirectly reflecting microcirculation perfusion, but the consistency relationship between the two is affected by the complexity of AKI [64].

The development of ultrasound contrast media and the corresponding software for contrast quantification has opened possibilities for novel and noninvasive means of measuring perfusion directly [62–66]. Ultrasound contrast consists of microbubbles, which remain entirely intravascular throughout their lifespan and are not affected by glomerular filtration or tubular transport [66]. The bubbles have rheology and a size like that of red blood cells and are used for perfusion analysis in various organs. During CEUS, the use of intravenous contrast product increases the blood echogenicity and enhances the visualization of microcirculatory renal perfusion during an ultrasound examination. A good correlation was observed between CEUS measurements and gold standard renal blood flow measurements (para-aminohippurate clearance) [67].

#### Examination method

#### Common indicators

The quantitative indicators reflect the volume of microcirculation blood perfusion and blood flow velocity in microcirculation, including mechanical index, region of interest (ROI), acoustic intensity (AI), microvascular blood volume (MBV), microvascular blood flow (MBF), microvascular flow velocity (MFV), rise time (RT), wash in slope (WIS), time to peak (TTP), mean transit time (MTT), peak intensity (PI), time-intensity curves (TIC), and area under the curve (AUC). PI, AUC, and MBV reflect the volume of microcirculatory perfusion. RT, TTP, MTT, WIS, and MFV reflect the blood flow velocity in the microcirculation.

#### Contrast agent infusion mode

CEUS can be performed using a continuous microbubble infusion or by injection of a single bolus [68] (Figure 7).

*Figure 7.: Continuous infusion or single bolus time-intensity curve obtained by contrast medium infusion [68]. flash-replenishment and time-intensity curve. (A) flash-replenishment curve during continuous perfusion. The curve starts after microbubble destruction. Time in second(s) is displayed on the horizontal axis, while the AI in au on the vertical axis. After microbubble destruction, microbubble tissue replenishment showed an exponential curve and obtained using the corresponding formula: video intensity (VI) = MBV (1− e−MFV(t−0.5)). maximal AI after complete filling of the microvascular bed is a parameter of MBV, while the slope of the initial increase is a parameter of MFV. (B) TIC obtained after a bolus injection of ultrasound contrast agent. Time in second(s) is displayed on the horizontal axis, while the AI in au on the vertical axis. PI and AUC are parameters of MBV, while MTT is a parameter of MVF.*

Continuous microbubble infusion results in a steady state microbubble concentration (Figure 7A). A SonoVue dose of 2.4 mL/bottle is often selected and pumped at a rate of 1 mL/min after dilution with an equal amount of normal saline. Bolus administration (Figure 7B) produces a rapid increase in the contrast agent concentration and signal followed by a slower contrast washout and is the most common form of contrast agent administration for nondestructive imaging. A bolus injection should be immediately followed by the administration of 5–10 mL saline bolus to flush the line at the same speed at which the contrast agent was infused. High pressure should be avoided because it may lead to the destruction of microbubbles.

#### Clinical application

CEUS has the potential to allow clinicians to see the renal perfusion real-time, allowing rapid assessment of the efficacy of therapeutic interventions in individual patients at bedside.

For example, the perfusion indexes such as PI and AUC were decreased, while the perfusion pressure (MAP-CVP) and CO were normal or even higher than normal, indicating that the precapillary arteriole was more likely to shrink if combined with increased RRI; it is more likely to be associated with inflammation, strong stressors or high levels of vasopressors. At this time, MAP should be titrated by adjusting the dose of vasopressors according to PI and AUC, and strategies can be adopted to reduce inflammation and stress level, such as optimizing analgesic and sedation strategies. If combined with discontinuous renal vein waveform, which indicates that the renal microcirculation stasis induced by increased renal afterload may play a certain role in it, and CVP should be reduced simultaneously or first. While, if the decreased perfusion was associated with insufficient perfusion pressure or CO, the causes of insufficient MAP and CO should be found and resolved, and then renal microcirculation perfusion should be evaluated again.

Microcirculation blood flow velocity is generally a sensitive indicator reflecting microcirculation perfusion. Patients with early sepsis generally show increased blood flow velocity and decreased RT and MTT. If RT and MTT and other indicators are prolonged, it indicates the possibility of vasoconstriction regardless of the PI and AUC.

Of note, although the prominent role of the CEUS, the use of it to guide renal perfusion resuscitation needs further investigation.

### Evaluation

Evaluation means interpreting ultrasound results and integrating them with clinical information to make clinical judgments and treatment decisions. Evaluation is dynamic and continuous and should be conducted during each step throughout the whole protocol. At the end of the protocol, a final comprehensive evaluation is required.

## Advantages of CCUSG-A(KI)BCDE protocol

First, this protocol is the first protocol to use bedside ultrasound to comprehensively evaluate renal hemodynamics. Each step contains a rich connotation of the critical illness, which presents the renal tissue structure and renal blood perfusion, morphology and function, physiology and pathology, medical history and etiology in front of the clinicians continuously and dynamically. Second, this protocol has noninvasive, convenient, real-time, dynamic, and economical features, thus enabling individualized and organ-target diagnosis and treatment at the bedside. At last, this protocol is an example of the organic integration of critical care medicine and POCUS, which was completed under the guidance of the principle of critical illness.

## Disadvantages

First, the completion of this protocol requires solid basic skills of critical ultrasound and profound knowledge of pathophysiology. Incorrect acquisition and interpretation of ultrasound sections will lead to incorrect clinical judgment. However, this is true of every laboratory examination and monitoring technique.

And there is still a lack of research data to support the efficacy of the CCUSG-A(KI)BCDE protocol; our clinical randomized trial on this protocol is still in progress at the moment, and a large-scale of sample, multi-center clinical randomized trial will be conducted in the future.

## Conclusion

The CCUSG-A(KI)BCDE procedure is a bedside ultrasound examination that examines the morphology and blood flow of the kidneys. Combined with the patient’s current and past medical history, this method can be used for comprehensive evaluation of the renal hemodynamics and acquisition and analysis of the pathophysiological mechanisms of the occurrence and progression of AKI; therefore, the occurrence and progression of AKI can be predicted, and targeted, individualized AKI diagnosis and treatment based on the pathophysiological mechanisms can be implemented; such management strategy should be promoted and implemented in the clinical setting.
